result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B is narrowly better. Its plan matches the intended order: define tokens first, then collapse near-duplicates (keeping the old class names as aliases to avoid touching markup), then change components. Its radius scale also keeps modals and panels separate from controls instead of flattening them. A is more candid that it has only seen one excerpt and is right that merging colours will barely show, but it merges near-duplicates before defining the scales. B contradicts itself by calling two different steps the 'most visible' change, and neither answer clearly says which differences, such as modal elevation, are intentional. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): B quotes more of the actual values: the full padding and margin spread, all three shadows, and the 17px shared by the big button and h4. It also gives a concrete token block with target values and is more honest about its limits: it suggests checking usage first, says it has seen only one excerpt, and says to confirm the gray in a contrast checker. Neither answer clearly separates accidental differences from intentional ones. Both state contrast ratios with confidence, and B also guesses that contrast is what users would notice most. A orders the work better (tokens first) and is more concise, but it calls the color merge both the most visible change and the lowest-risk one, which is confusing.
